stem: In the Next.js App Router, which of these can a Server Component do that a Client Component cannot?

options.text: Hold local state with `useState` and update it when a button is clicked
options.why: State and event handlers need the component to run in the browser, which Server Components never do.

options.text: Query the database directly in its body, with no API endpoint
options.why: Server Component code runs only on the server, so it can read databases, files and secrets during render.

options.text: Read `window.localStorage` during render to restore a saved preference
options.why: There is no `window` on the server; browser APIs belong in Client Components (and usually in effects).

options.text: Attach an `onClick` handler to a button and respond to the click
options.why: Event handlers are functions that must run in the browser, so they need a Client Component.

explanation: Server Components run only on the server (at build time or per request) and their code never ships to the browser. That lets them read data sources and secrets directly. In exchange they cannot use state, effects, event handlers or browser APIs, which need the component to run on the client.

stem: A component exported from a file that starts with `'use client'` is never rendered on the server.

options.text: True
options.why: It is still rendered on the server to produce the initial HTML, then hydrated in the browser.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: Client Components are server-rendered for the first load and also run in the browser.

explanation: `'use client'` marks a boundary between the server and client module graphs; it does not mean "render only in the browser". On a direct visit a Client Component renders on the server to HTML and again in the browser during hydration. The difference from a Server Component is that its code also ships to, and runs in, the browser.
reference: Next.js docs: The Server and Client Boundary

stem: Where must the `'use client'` directive go for it to take effect?

options.text: Inside the component function body, as its first statement
options.why: That position is valid for `'use server'` inside an async function, not for `'use client'`.

options.text: At the very top of the module, before any imports
options.why: The directive marks the whole module, so it must come first (only comments may precede it).

options.text: Directly above the `export default` line of the component it marks
options.why: A directive in the middle of a module is just an unused string expression and has no effect.

options.text: In `next.config.js`, listing the files that should become Client Components
options.why: There is no such config list; the boundary is declared in each module with the directive.

explanation: `'use client'` is a module-level directive. It must be the first statement in the file, before imports; comments are allowed above it. It marks the module (and everything it imports) as part of the client module graph.

stem: In the App Router, components are Server Components by default. Type the directive string you put at the top of a file so its exports become Client Component entry points (without quotes).
explanation: Adding `'use client'` at the top of a module makes its exports entry points into the client module graph. You only need it on files whose components are rendered directly by Server Components; anything those files import is already client code.

stem: Which of these is a valid Server Component in the App Router?

options.text: `export default async function Page() { const posts = await getPosts(); return <List posts={posts} /> }`
options.why: Server Components may be async and await data directly during render.

options.text: `export default function Page() { const [posts, setPosts] = useState([]); return <List posts={posts} /> }`
options.why: useState is a client-only hook; a Server Component cannot hold state.

options.text: `export default function Page() { useEffect(() => { load() }, []); return <List /> }`
options.why: Effects run after a component mounts in the browser, which never happens for Server Components.

options.text: `export default function Page() { return <button onClick={() => alert(1)}>Hi</button> }`
options.why: Passing an event handler requires a Client Component, because the handler must run in the browser.

explanation: Server Components can be `async` functions that `await` data. Hooks such as useState and useEffect, and event handlers, all need the component to run in the browser, so they are only allowed in Client Components.

stem: Match each piece of code with where it is allowed to run in the App Router.

options.text: Server Components only
Client Components only
Both Server and Client Components

prompts.text: An `async` component that awaits a database query in its body

Rendering plain JSX such as `

{title}

` from props
Reading `process.env.STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` (no `NEXT_PUBLIC_` prefix) to call an API

explanation: State hooks need the browser, so they are client-only. Async components and server secrets are server-only: Client Component code is shipped to the browser, where non-public environment variables are not available. Plain JSX from props works in either environment.
reference: Next.js docs: Server and Client Components

stem: What does adding `import 'server-only'` to the top of `lib/dal.ts` do in a Next.js app?

options.text: It encrypts the module so that its source is unreadable in the browser bundle
options.why: Nothing is encrypted; the point is that the module must never reach the browser bundle at all.

options.text: It makes the build fail if any Client Component module imports `lib/dal.ts`
options.why: It turns accidental client imports of server code into a build-time error.

options.text: It turns every exported function into a Server Action callable from the client
options.why: That is what `'use server'` does. `server-only` creates no endpoints.

options.text: It runs the module once at build time and caches the result for every request
options.why: It has no effect on caching or when the code runs.

explanation: `server-only` guards against "environment poisoning": if a module that reads secrets or the database is imported into the client module graph, the build fails instead of silently bundling it. Next.js handles the import internally, and `client-only` is the mirror image for browser-only code.

options.text: It works, and the log line appears in the browser console when an item is selected
options.why: Functions cannot cross from server to client as props, so the arrow function never reaches the browser.

options.text: It works, and the log line appears in the server terminal when an item is selected
options.why: The browser has no way to call back into a plain server function; only Server Functions get an endpoint.

options.text: Rendering fails: a plain function is not a serializable prop
options.why: Props crossing the boundary must be serializable, and ordinary functions are not.

options.text: It works only after wrapping the arrow function in `useCallback` inside the page
options.why: Hooks are not allowed in Server Components, and memoising would not make the function serializable.

explanation: Props passed from a Server Component to a Client Component are serialized into the RSC payload. Plain functions cannot be serialized, so React throws ("Functions cannot be passed directly to Client Components…"). Either define the handler inside the Client Component, or pass a Server Function (marked `'use server'`), which is sent as a reference.

stem: A Server Component renders `<Chart data={x} />`, where Chart is a Client Component. Which values of `x` can be passed as that prop? (Choose three.)

options.text: A `Date` object
options.why: Dates are on the list of serializable types and arrive as Date objects.

options.text: A pending `Promise` that resolves to an array of numbers
options.why: Promises are serializable; the client can read them with `use` while a Suspense boundary waits.

options.text: A `Map` from string keys to numbers
options.why: Maps and Sets are supported iterables, as are arrays and typed arrays.

options.text: An instance of a custom `Money` class
options.why: Class instances (other than built-ins) are not serializable; convert them to plain objects first.

options.text: An arrow function that formats each point
options.why: Plain functions cannot cross the boundary unless they are Server Functions.

options.text: An object created with `Object.create(null)`
options.why: Null-prototype objects are explicitly listed as unsupported.

explanation: React can serialize primitives, plain objects and arrays, Dates, Maps, Sets, typed arrays, Promises, JSX elements and Server Functions. Class instances, null-prototype objects, unregistered symbols and ordinary functions cannot be passed to Client Components.

stem: In a Next.js app, `components/sidebar.jsx` starts with `'use client'` and imports `./ads.jsx`, which has no directive and renders `process.env.ADS_PARTNER_ID`. Ads is only ever rendered by Sidebar. What is the result?

options.text: Ads stays a Server Component because its own file has no `'use client'` directive
options.why: A file's directive is not the only factor: anything imported from a client module joins the client graph.

options.text: Ads becomes browser code, where the non-public variable is undefined
options.why: Imports from a client module are client code, and only NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables are inlined for the browser.

options.text: The build fails, because a module without a directive cannot be imported by a client module
options.why: Undirected modules can be imported anywhere; they simply take on the environment of their importer.

options.text: Next.js renders Ads on the server and streams it into Sidebar as a separate payload chunk
options.why: Only Server Components passed as props or children are rendered on the server; imports are bundled.

explanation: `'use client'` marks an entry point, and everything that module imports becomes part of the client module graph. Ads is therefore bundled for the browser. In client code Next.js only inlines `NEXT_PUBLIC_` variables, so `process.env.ADS_PARTNER_ID` is undefined in the browser. The server render would still see the value, which can also cause a hydration mismatch. Read such values on the server and pass them down, or render Ads as a child from a Server Component.
reference: Next.js docs: Server and Client Components; Environment Variables

stem: A Client Component `Modal` renders `{children}` inside a dialog. A Server Component page renders `<Modal><CartSummary /></Modal>`, where CartSummary is an async Server Component that reads the database. What happens?

options.text: CartSummary becomes a Client Component because it is rendered inside a Client Component
options.why: Nesting by composition does not change a component's environment; only imports into client modules do.

options.text: It fails, because Client Components cannot receive Server Components in any form
options.why: Passing Server Components as children or props is the recommended way to compose them with client UI.

options.text: CartSummary renders on the server, and Modal receives its rendered output as `children`
options.why: The page renders CartSummary first, and Modal gets the result as a serialized JSX prop.

options.text: CartSummary renders twice: once on the server and again in the browser when Modal mounts
options.why: Server Component code never runs in the browser; the client only sees its rendered result.

explanation: The page (a Server Component) owns the JSX `<CartSummary />`, so React renders it on the server and passes the result into Modal as `children`. Modal never imports CartSummary, so it stays a Server Component and can keep reading the database. This "slot" pattern is how you place server-rendered content inside interactive client wrappers.
reference: react.dev: 'use client' (passing Server Components as props)

options.text: `useFormStatus` only works when the form's action is a Server Function defined inline in the file
options.why: It works with any form action, including imported Server Functions and client functions.

options.text: It reads the parent `<form>`, and this component has no parent form
options.why: Move the button into a child component rendered inside the form and call the hook there.

options.text: The form needs `method="post"`, otherwise React submits it as a normal GET navigation
options.why: React handles function actions itself; the method attribute does not affect `pending`.

options.text: `pending` only becomes true after hydration completes, so it is always false during server rendering
options.why: This form is interactive and hydrated; the issue is where the hook is called, not when.

explanation: `useFormStatus` reads the status of the nearest enclosing `<form>`, as if the form were a context provider. Called in the same component that renders the form, there is no parent form, so `pending` is always false. The fix is a small `SubmitButton` component that calls `useFormStatus` and is rendered inside the form.

options.text: Server Functions receive a plain object, not FormData, so `.get` does not exist on it
options.why: Form actions do receive FormData; the problem is which argument holds it.

options.text: The form needs `encType="multipart/form-data"` before the action receives FormData
options.why: React builds the FormData itself for function actions; no encType is required.

options.text: With `useActionState`, the action receives the previous state first and FormData second
options.why: Here `formData` is actually `null` (the initial state); change the signature to `(prevState, formData)`.

options.text: `subscribe` must be marked `'use server'` inside its body as well as at the top of the file
options.why: The file-level directive already makes every export a Server Function.

explanation: `useActionState(action, initialState)` calls the action as `action(previousState, payload)`. On the first submit `previousState` is the initial state (`null` here) and the FormData arrives as the second argument. Update the action to `async function subscribe(prevState, formData)` and return the next state.

stem: Hiding the Delete button from non-admin users is enough to protect the `deleteUser` Server Action that the button calls.

options.text: True
options.why: Hiding UI does not stop someone sending the same request directly.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: every Server Action is a public POST endpoint, so it must check authorization itself.

explanation: A Server Action is invoked with a POST request carrying its action ID, and anyone who can send that request can call it, with or without your UI. Render-time gating is not a security boundary. Every action must authenticate the caller and check they may perform this operation on this resource.

options.text: About 500 ms, because React runs the awaits in a Server Component in parallel automatically
options.why: Each `await` pauses the function, so the second request only starts after the first finishes.

options.text: About 800 ms; start both requests first and await them with `Promise.all` to get about 500 ms
options.why: Sequential awaits form a waterfall; starting both promises before awaiting overlaps them.

options.text: About 800 ms, and nothing helps, because Server Components can only await one promise at a time
options.why: Server Components are ordinary async functions and can await `Promise.all` like any other.

options.text: About 300 ms, because Next.js streams the page as soon as the first request resolves
options.why: Streaming needs Suspense boundaries; this component awaits both before returning any JSX.

explanation: Two sequential awaits create a request waterfall: 300 + 500 = 800 ms. When the requests are independent, start both and await them together: `const [user, feed] = await Promise.all([getUser(), getFeed()])` takes about max(300, 500) = 500 ms. To show part of the page sooner, move each await into its own component under a Suspense boundary.
reference: Next.js docs: Fetching Data (parallel data fetching)

stem: A layout wants every component below it to read the current theme. A teammate writes `const theme = useContext(ThemeContext)` inside an async Server Component, and it errors. Which two changes are valid fixes? (Choose two.)

options.text: Create a `'use client'` ThemeProvider that renders the context provider around `{children}`
options.why: Server Components can render a client provider and pass server content through it as children.

options.text: Read the theme with `useContext` in a Client Component somewhere below that provider
options.why: Context is a client feature, so consumers must be Client Components.

options.text: Mark the async Server Component with `'use server'` so it is allowed to call hooks
options.why: `'use server'` marks Server Functions; it never enables hooks in components.

options.text: Wrap the `useContext` call in `React.cache()` so it runs once per request
options.why: `cache` memoises data functions and does not make context available on the server.

options.text: Call `React.createContext` inside the Server Component so each request gets its own context
options.why: Creating context in a Server Component does not help; it still cannot read context.

explanation: React context is not available in Server Components. The standard pattern is a small Client Component provider (for example ThemeProvider) that the server layout renders around `{children}`. Server Components inside still render on the server, and any Client Component below the provider can read the value with `useContext`. To share data between Server Components, use props or `cache()`.
reference: Next.js docs: Server and Client Components (context providers)

stem: `useActionState` returns a tuple. The first element is the current state and the second is the action to pass to the form. Type the conventional name of the boolean returned as the third element.
explanation: `const [state, formAction, isPending] = useActionState(action, initialState)`. `isPending` is true while the action is running, so you can disable the button or show a spinner without a separate `useFormStatus` child.

stem: In Next.js, environment variables are only available on the server unless their name starts with a special prefix, in which case their values are inlined into client JavaScript at build time. Type that prefix.
explanation: Only variables named `NEXT_PUBLIC_…` are inlined into the browser bundle at build time. Everything else stays server-side, which is why Client Components see `undefined` for secrets. Never prefix a secret with `NEXT_PUBLIC_`.

stem: A user submits a `<form action={createPost}>`. The Server Action inserts a row and calls `revalidatePath('/posts')`. Put the steps in the order they happen in the Next.js App Router.

options.text: The browser sends a POST with the action ID and the form's FormData
The server runs `createPost` with the FormData
`revalidatePath` invalidates the cached data for `/posts`
The server re-renders the current route to a fresh RSC payload
One response streams the action's return value and the new payload, and the client updates the UI

explanation: Server Actions are POST requests that reference the action by ID. When an action triggers revalidation, Next.js does everything in one round trip: it runs the action, invalidates the affected data, re-renders the route on the server, and streams the return value plus the new RSC payload back in the same response.
reference: Next.js docs: Server Actions (single round trip)

options.text: It never leaves the server: the action runs inside the same closure on the server when clicked
options.why: The page has finished rendering by the time the button is clicked, so that closure no longer exists.

options.text: It is sent to the browser in plain text inside the form markup and posted back unchanged
options.why: Next.js encrypts closed-over values before sending them; they are not plain text.

options.text: It is serialized, encrypted into the page and posted back with the action call
options.why: Captured variables are a snapshot taken at render time and are encrypted by Next.js.

options.text: It causes a build error, because inline Server Actions cannot close over outer variables
options.why: Closures are allowed; capturing a snapshot of render-time data is a documented use case.

explanation: An inline Server Action that closes over variables needs those values when it is invoked later, so Next.js serializes the captured values, encrypts them, and round-trips them through the client. That is handy for snapshots like `version`, but don't capture secrets: read them inside the action instead. Self-hosted deployments with several instances should set a shared `NEXT_SERVER_ACTIONS_ENCRYPTION_KEY`.
reference: Next.js docs: Data Security (closures and encryption)

stem:
After this action runs, the user lands on `/posts` but the new post is missing until they reload. Why?

```jsx
'use server'
import { redirect } from 'next/navigation'
import { revalidatePath } from 'next/cache'

export async function createPost(formData) {
  await db.post.create({ data: { title: formData.get('title') } })
  redirect('/posts')
  revalidatePath('/posts')
}
```

options.text: `revalidatePath` only works inside Route Handlers, not inside Server Actions
options.why: Server Actions are a primary place to call revalidatePath.

options.text: `redirect` throws a control-flow exception, so the `revalidatePath` line never runs
options.why: Call revalidatePath before redirect when the destination needs fresh data.

options.text: The database write is not awaited, so it commits after the redirect has already rendered
options.why: The create call is awaited; the problem is the line after redirect.

options.text: `redirect` from a Server Action always performs a full page reload that skips the cache
options.why: Action redirects navigate the client router and stream the destination; they don't bypass caches.

explanation: `redirect()` works by throwing a special error that Next.js catches to perform the navigation. Code after it never runs, so the revalidation is skipped and `/posts` is served from the stale cache. Put `revalidatePath` (or `updateTag`) before `redirect`.

options.text: It never checks who is calling or whether they may change roles
options.why: The action is a public POST endpoint, so anyone can grant themselves admin.

options.text: It returns the whole user record, including fields like the password hash, to the client
options.why: Return values are serialized to the browser; return only what the UI needs.

options.text: Server Actions must be GET requests, so a mutation like this should be a Route Handler
options.why: Actions are POST requests, and mutations are their main use case.

options.text: The `'use server'` directive must be inside the function body, not at the top of the file
options.why: A file-level directive is valid and marks every export as a Server Function.

options.text: The `userId` argument is visible in transit because Next.js does not use HTTPS for actions
options.why: Transport security comes from your deployment; the bugs are missing auth and over-returning data.

explanation: Treat every Server Action like a public API route. Validate the input (role should be an allowed value), authenticate the caller, and authorize the specific change, ideally through a server-only data access layer. Shape the return value to the UI, because whatever you return is serialized to the client.
reference: Next.js docs: Server Actions (Security); Data Security

stem: A post page should show its body immediately and stream the slow comments in later. Which version achieves that?

options.text: Page does `const comments = await getComments(id)` and then renders `<Suspense><Comments comments={comments} /></Suspense>`
options.why: The page awaits the comments before returning, so the whole response waits for them.

options.text: Page renders `<Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}><Comments promise={getComments(id)} /></Suspense>`; Comments calls `use(promise)`
options.why: The fetch starts on the server without blocking, and Suspense streams the comments when they resolve.

options.text: Comments is a Client Component that calls `fetch('/api/comments')` in a `useEffect` after it mounts
options.why: This works, but the request only starts after hydration, which is later than starting it on the server.

options.text: Page wraps the post body in `<Suspense>` and awaits the comments at the top of the page component
options.why: Suspense around content that is already available does nothing; the top-level await still blocks.

explanation: Start the request in the Server Component without awaiting it, and pass the pending promise to a component under a Suspense boundary. The shell streams immediately with the fallback, and the comments stream in when the promise resolves, read with `use(promise)` in a Client Component or awaited in an async Server Component.
reference: react.dev: use (streaming data from server to client)

options.text: `use` can only read promises inside Server Components, so in a Client Component it never resolves
options.why: `use` works in Client Components; the problem is where this promise is created.

options.text: A new promise is created on every render, so each render suspends again on a fresh, uncached promise
options.why: Create the promise outside render (in a Server Component, a cache or a data library) and pass it in.

options.text: The fetch is missing `{ cache: 'force-cache' }`, so the browser discards the response before React reads it
options.why: Browser fetch caching has nothing to do with it; React needs the same promise object across renders.

options.text: `use` must be called inside a `useEffect`, because it is a side effect
options.why: `use` is called during render, like other hooks, but unlike them it may be conditional.

explanation: When a component suspends, React throws away that render and tries again when the promise settles. If the promise is created inside render, the retry creates a brand-new pending promise and suspends again. React warns that uncached promises created in Client Components are not supported. Create the promise in a Server Component and pass it as a prop, or use a cache or data library that returns the same promise.

options.text: `cache` only works for `fetch` calls, not for database queries
options.why: React `cache` memoises any function; it is not limited to fetch.

options.text: Each `cache()` call creates a separate cache, so nothing is shared
options.why: Define `const getUser = cache(fetchUserFromDb)` once at module level and import it.

options.text: `cache` keys on the function's source text, and the two components are in different files
options.why: It keys on the memoised function's identity and its arguments, not on source text.

options.text: `cache` lasts for one render of one component, so it can never share data across components
options.why: It lasts for a whole server request, which is exactly how it shares results between components.

explanation: React `cache(fn)` returns a memoised version of `fn`, and each call to `cache` creates a separate cache. Creating it inside a component gives every component (and every render) its own empty cache. Create the cached function once at module scope and call it from any Server Component; calls with the same arguments in the same request then share one result.

stem: A team wraps an expensive stats query with React `cache` at module level, expecting it to stop hitting the database on every page view. Each visit still runs the query. Why?

options.text: Module-level `cache` is disabled in production builds and only works in development
options.why: It works the same in production; its scope is simply smaller than they assumed.

options.text: React `cache` lasts for one server request; each request starts empty
options.why: For data that should persist across requests, use framework caching (in Next.js, Cache Components or `use cache`).

options.text: The query has no arguments, and `cache` only memoises functions that take arguments
options.why: Zero-argument functions are memoised too; there is just one cache entry.

options.text: `cache` is ignored unless the query function returns a Promise of JSON-serializable data
options.why: Serializability doesn't matter for `cache`; it stores whatever the function returns.

explanation: React `cache` is per-request memoisation: it dedupes calls within one server render and is cleared when that request ends. Caching results across requests and users is a framework concern. In Next.js 16 that means Cache Components (`'use cache'` with cacheLife and cacheTag) or, for fetch, persistent fetch caching.

stem: In a Next.js production build, every exported async function in a `'use server'` file gets a public endpoint, even one that no component ever imports or calls.

options.text: True
options.why: Next.js strips unused Server Functions, so they never get an endpoint.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: unused Server Functions are dead-code eliminated, so only the ones actually referenced become reachable.

explanation: At build time Next.js replaces each Server Function referenced from client code with an encrypted, non-deterministic action ID, and strips unused ones so they have no public endpoint. Every action that is used is still reachable by anyone who can send the POST, so it must do its own authentication and authorization.
reference: Next.js docs: Data Security (built-in Server Actions security)

stem:
A Client Component renders `

Rendered at {new Date().toLocaleTimeString()}

`. On a direct visit, React reports a hydration error. What is the best fix?

options.text: Convert it to a Server Component so that it only renders once and never hydrates
options.why: Then the time is fixed at render and never updates, and it can't be interactive.

options.text: Show the time only after mount (via `useEffect`), or use `suppressHydrationWarning`
options.why: Hydration needs the first client render to match the server HTML; client-only values must come after mount.

options.text: Wrap the paragraph in `<Suspense>` so that React re-renders it on the client without comparing
options.why: Suspense does not exempt content from hydration matching.

options.text: Use `Date.now()` instead of `toLocaleTimeString()` so that the server and browser produce identical numbers
options.why: The server and browser run at different moments, so any current-time value differs.

explanation: A Client Component renders twice on a direct visit: on the server to make HTML, and in the browser during hydration. The two renders must produce the same output. Values that differ by time, locale or randomness should be shown after mount (state set in an effect). For a single text node that is expected to differ, `suppressHydrationWarning` silences the warning.
reference: react.dev: hydrateRoot (handling different client and server content)

stem: Match each rendering term with what it describes in the Next.js App Router.

options.text: Static Site Generation (SSG)
Incremental Static Regeneration (ISR)
Server-side rendering (SSR)
React Server Components (RSC)

prompts.text: HTML is produced once at build time and reused for every visitor
Pre-rendered HTML is regenerated after the build, on a schedule or on demand
HTML is produced on the server for each incoming request
Component code stays on the server and the output is sent as a serialized payload

explanation: "Server-rendered" describes how and when HTML is produced (build time, after build, or per request). "Server Component" describes where a component's code runs and whether it ships to the browser. A route can use RSC together with SSG, ISR or SSR; they answer different questions.
reference: Next.js docs: The Server and Client Boundary

stem: What does the RSC payload that the server sends to the browser contain? (Choose two.)

options.text: The rendered output of the Server Components in the tree
options.why: Server Components are sent as their result, not as code.

options.text: References to Client Components (their bundle chunks) together with their serialized props
options.why: The client uses these references to load and render Client Components.

options.text: The JavaScript source code of every Server Component, so the browser can re-render them later
options.why: Server Component code never reaches the browser; that is the point of RSC.

options.text: Only the final HTML string, which the browser inserts with `innerHTML`
options.why: HTML is a separate output; the payload is a serialized React tree used for hydration and navigation.

options.text: The database queries the Server Components ran, so the browser can repeat them offline
options.why: Queries run only on the server; only their rendered results and serialized props are sent.

explanation: The RSC payload is a compact serialized description of the rendered tree. It holds Server Component output, placeholders that reference Client Component code, and the props passed to them. On the initial load it ships with the HTML. On client-side navigations the server sends only a new payload, which React reconciles into the page.
reference: Next.js docs: The Server and Client Boundary (RSC payload)

stem: A file starts with `'use server'` and contains `export const MAX_ITEMS = 50` alongside two exported async actions. What happens?

options.text: It works: the constant is sent to the client as a serialized value next to the action references
options.why: Exports of a `'use server'` file become callable references, which a constant cannot be.

options.text: It is an error, because a `'use server'` file may only export async functions
options.why: Move shared constants to a normal module and import them where needed.

options.text: The constant is silently dropped from the module, and importing it anywhere gives `undefined`
options.why: The compiler reports an error rather than silently dropping the export.

options.text: It works, but MAX_ITEMS is turned into an async function that returns 50 when called
options.why: React never wraps non-function exports into functions.

explanation: Every export of a `'use server'` module becomes a Server Function reference that the client can call over the network, so React and Next.js only allow async functions to be exported. Constants, types (at runtime) and synchronous helpers belong in a separate module, which can be marked `server-only` if it must not reach the client.

stem: A Server Component imports `logView` from a `'use server'` file and calls `await logView(slug)` during render. What happens?

options.text: React sends a POST request to its own server to invoke the action, which adds a network hop
options.why: On the server, a Server Function is just an async function and is called directly.

options.text: It runs as an ordinary async function call on the server, with no network request
options.why: The `'use server'` boundary only matters when client code invokes the function.

options.text: It throws, because Server Actions can only be invoked from forms or Client Components
options.why: They can be called from Server Components too; they just aren't endpoints in that case.

options.text: It is deferred until after the response has streamed, like an analytics beacon sent from the page
options.why: Awaiting it blocks the render like any other awaited call; deferral needs `after()` or similar.

explanation: `'use server'` tells the bundler to give client code a reference that POSTs to the server. Server Components already run on the server, so importing and calling the function is a plain async call. For work that shouldn't block the response, such as logging, Next.js provides `after()`.

stem: A user opens a Next.js App Router page directly (not a client-side navigation). The page has Server and Client Components. Put these steps in order.

options.text: The server renders the Server Components into the RSC payload
The server uses the payload and the Client Components to render HTML
The browser receives and paints the HTML before any React code runs
The browser loads the Client Component JavaScript
React hydrates the page using the RSC payload, attaching event handlers

explanation: On a direct visit, Server Components render first to the RSC payload. Next.js then renders HTML from that payload plus the Client Components, so the browser can paint quickly. After the client JavaScript loads, React hydrates, reconciling the payload with the existing HTML and attaching interactivity.
reference: Next.js docs: Server and Client Components (how they work)

options.text: `redirect` cannot be called inside an action used with `useActionState`, so React rejects it
options.why: Redirecting from such an action is supported; the problem is the surrounding try/catch.

options.text: `redirect` works by throwing, and the `catch` swallows that signal
options.why: Call redirect after the try/catch, or rethrow framework errors (for example with `unstable_rethrow`).

options.text: The insert is rolled back because `redirect` aborts the request before the transaction commits
options.why: The create was awaited and committed before redirect ran.

options.text: `post.id` is undefined inside the try block, so redirect throws a TypeError
options.why: The ID comes from the awaited create; the thrown value is the redirect signal itself.

explanation: `redirect()` (like `notFound()`) works by throwing a special error that Next.js handles. A broad `try/catch` intercepts it, and the action returns the error state instead of navigating. Keep `redirect` outside the try block, or rethrow Next.js control-flow errors in the catch.

stem:
A like button uses `useOptimistic`. Which statements are true? (Choose three.)

```jsx
const [optimisticLikes, addOptimistic] = useOptimistic(
  likes,
  (current, delta) => current + delta
)
```

options.text: When the action or transition finishes, the value goes back to whatever `likes` is at that point
options.why: Optimistic state is temporary and is replaced by the real state when the action settles.

options.text: `addOptimistic` must be called inside an action or `startTransition`
options.why: Outside a transition React warns, and the optimistic update is shown and then immediately reverted.

options.text: The update function receives the current state and the value passed to `addOptimistic`
options.why: It works like a reducer: (currentState, optimisticValue) => nextOptimisticState.

options.text: If the Server Action throws, the optimistic value stays on screen until the page reloads
options.why: It reverts when the action settles either way, so a failed save shows the old count again.

options.text: It only works in Server Components, since it is designed for Server Actions
options.why: It is a client hook, used in Client Components.

options.text: It replaces the need to update `likes` after the server confirms the change
options.why: If `likes` never changes, the optimistic value disappears and the old count comes back.

explanation: `useOptimistic(state, updateFn)` shows a temporary value while an async action is pending. Once the action or transition completes, React renders with the real `state` again. If the server confirmed the change (for example via revalidation or new props), the UI stays updated; if it failed, it reverts. Calls must happen inside an action or transition.

stem: In the Next.js App Router, a client handler runs `await Promise.all([star(a), star(b), star(c)])`, where each Server Action takes about 400 ms. The UI takes about 1.2 s to settle. Why?

options.text: Promise.all runs promises one after another when they come from Server Actions
options.why: Promise.all never serializes work; the ordering comes from how Next.js dispatches actions.

options.text: Next.js dispatches Server Actions one at a time per client, so the three calls queue
options.why: Do the work in a single action that parallelises on the server, or use a Route Handler for non-mutations.

options.text: Each action re-renders the page, and React cannot overlap renders, so they block each other
options.why: Rendering is not the bottleneck; the client queues the requests before they are even sent.

options.text: Browsers allow only one POST at a time per origin, so the requests cannot overlap
options.why: Browsers allow several concurrent requests per origin; the queueing is in the framework.

explanation: Next.js dispatches Server Actions sequentially per client, so that the re-rendered server tree always matches the result of the action that produced it. `Promise.all` over actions therefore takes the sum of their durations. If you need parallel work, do it inside one action (for example `Promise.all` on the server), fetch in a Server Component, or call a Route Handler.
reference: Next.js docs: Server Actions (sequential dispatch on the client)

stem: `components/index.js` re-exports `Chart` (a `'use client'` component) and `ReportTable` (a Server Component that imports `'server-only'` and queries the database). A Client Component does `import { Chart } from '@/components'`. What is the most likely result?

options.text: It works: tree shaking removes ReportTable before the server-only check ever runs
options.why: The check runs as the module graph is built, so the barrel's import of ReportTable is still processed.

options.text: The build fails, because importing the barrel pulls ReportTable into the client graph
options.why: Import Chart from its own file, or keep separate client and server barrels.

options.text: ReportTable is silently converted to a Client Component and runs its query in the browser
options.why: `server-only` exists to turn exactly this into an error instead of a silent leak.

options.text: Next.js splits the barrel so that client imports get Chart and server imports get ReportTable
options.why: There is no automatic per-environment splitting of a single barrel module.

explanation: A client module that imports a barrel file pulls the barrel, and everything it re-exports, into the client module graph. ReportTable imports `server-only`, so the build fails with an error about importing a server-only module into a Client Component. Without `server-only`, the server code could have been bundled for the browser. Import client components from their own files, or keep separate client and server entry points.
reference: Next.js docs: Server and Client Components (preventing environment poisoning)

stem: `lib/format.js` starts with `'use client'` and exports both a `PriceTag` component and a helper `formatPrice(amount)`. A Server Component imports `formatPrice` and calls it during render. What happens?

options.text: It works normally, because `formatPrice` is a plain function with no hooks or browser APIs
options.why: Exports of a `'use client'` module are client references on the server, whatever they contain.

options.text: It throws: on the server the import is a client reference, which cannot be called there
options.why: Move shared helpers into a module without the directive and import it from both sides.

options.text: React serializes the call and runs `formatPrice` in the browser, then patches the result in
options.why: React never executes client functions on behalf of the server during rendering.

options.text: The build silently duplicates `formatPrice` into the server bundle, so the call succeeds
options.why: The directive makes every export of that module a client reference in the server graph.

explanation: In the server module graph, every export of a `'use client'` module is replaced by a client reference: something that can be rendered as a component or passed as a prop, but not executed. Calling it throws "Attempted to call formatPrice() from the server but formatPrice is on the client". Keep pure helpers in a module without a directive so both environments can import them.

stem:
A Server Component page renders: ```jsx Loading reviews…

}> {/* resolves after ~3 s */} Loading stock…

}> {/* resolves after ~1 s */} ``` With streaming SSR on a direct visit, what does the user see?

options.text: Both fallbacks until 3 s, then both sections at once, because the HTML streams in document order
options.why: React streams boundaries out of order, so a later section can resolve first.

options.text: Both fallbacks, then Stock at about 1 s and Reviews at about 3 s
options.why: Each boundary streams its HTML independently, and inline scripts swap it into place.

options.text: A blank page for 3 s, because the slowest boundary decides when the first byte is sent
options.why: The shell with both fallbacks is sent right away; that is what Suspense enables.

options.text: Stock at 1 s, and Reviews only after hydration finishes, because later boundaries render on the client
options.why: Both render on the server; Reviews streams from the server when its data resolves.

explanation: With streaming, React sends the shell, including fallbacks, immediately. When a boundary's content is ready, React streams its HTML at the end of the response together with a small inline script that moves it into the right place. Boundaries are independent and can resolve out of order, so Stock appears at about 1 s and Reviews at about 3 s. Hydration is also selective per boundary.
reference: react.dev: renderToPipeableStream (streaming more content as it loads)

options.text: Suspense fallbacks only appear on client-side navigations, never on a direct page load
options.why: Fallbacks stream in the initial HTML on direct loads too.

options.text: Page awaits above the boundary, so it suspends before Suspense renders
options.why: Move the await into a child under the boundary, or pass the promise down.

options.text: `Spinner` must be a Client Component to be used as a fallback
options.why: Fallbacks can be Server Components; any React node works.

options.text: PostList is synchronous, so there is nothing for this Suspense boundary to wait for
options.why: True, but the reason the page is blocked is the await above the boundary in Page.

explanation: A Suspense boundary only catches suspensions from components inside it. Here Page awaits before returning any JSX, so it suspends above the boundary. The nearest boundary above is the route's `loading.js` if there is one; without one, the whole response waits. Put the awaiting component inside the boundary (an async `<Posts />` that fetches its own data), or pass the un-awaited promise to it.

stem: In the Next.js App Router, a layout and a page both need the same user profile during one request. Which two approaches avoid querying twice, without prop drilling? (Choose two.)

options.text: Wrap the data function with React `cache()` at module level and call it from both
options.why: Calls with the same arguments in one request share a single result.

options.text: Use the same `fetch` GET URL and options in both, relying on fetch memoization within the render pass
options.why: Next.js memoizes identical GET fetches during a single server render pass.

options.text: Store the profile in a module-level `let` variable from the layout and read it in the page
options.why: Module state is shared by every concurrent request, so this leaks data between users.

options.text: Put the profile in React context in the layout and read it with `useContext` in the page
options.why: Server Components cannot read context.

options.text: Call the query inside `useMemo` in both components so React reuses the value
options.why: useMemo is a client hook and memoizes within one component instance only.

explanation: Within one server request, React `cache` dedupes calls to the same memoised function with the same arguments, and Next.js memoizes identical `fetch` GET requests during a render pass. Both let any component ask for data where it is needed instead of threading it through props. Neither persists across requests.

stem:
To avoid prop drilling, a team writes this module:

```jsx
// lib/request-user.js
let currentUser = null
export const setUser = (u) => { currentUser = u }
export const getUser = () => currentUser
```

The root layout calls `setUser(await auth())`, and deep Server Components call `getUser()`. In production, users occasionally see someone else's name. Why?

options.text: Server Components render in a random order, so `getUser` sometimes runs before `setUser`
options.why: Ordering would show null, not another user; the core problem is shared state.

options.text: Module state is shared by all concurrent requests, which overwrite it
options.why: Use per-request mechanisms: React `cache`, reading cookies or headers where needed, or props.

options.text: Next.js caches the root layout across users, so it always holds the first visitor's session
options.why: Layouts reading cookies render dynamically per request; the leak comes from the shared variable.

options.text: The variable is serialized into the RSC payload and reused by the browser for other users
options.why: Module variables are not serialized; this happens entirely within the server process.

explanation: A Node.js server handles many requests concurrently in one process, and module-level variables are shared by all of them. While one request awaits, another can call `setUser` and change what the first request reads, which is a cross-user data leak. Request-scoped data must be derived per request: call a `cache()`-wrapped `getCurrentUser()` that reads the session cookie wherever it is needed.
reference: react.dev: cache; Next.js docs: Data Security

stem: In Next.js 16, a Server Action updates a product and then calls `revalidateTag('products', 'max')`. The user is still shown the old product list in that same response. Why, and what should the action use if the user must see their own change immediately?

options.text: `revalidateTag` only works in Route Handlers; Server Actions must call `revalidatePath`
options.why: Both work in Server Actions; the profile decides how fresh the next read is.

options.text: With a stale-while-revalidate profile it only marks the tag for background refresh; use `updateTag` instead
options.why: updateTag (or revalidatePath) expires the data immediately so the re-render includes the change.

options.text: The action forgot to call `router.refresh()` from the server after revalidating
options.why: `router.refresh` is a client router method; the fix is the type of invalidation.

options.text: Cache tags only apply to `fetch` calls, so database reads are never revalidated by tag
options.why: Tagged `use cache` functions are revalidated by tag too; the stale profile is why it lags.

explanation: In Next.js 16, `revalidateTag` with a cache-life profile such as `'max'` is stale-while-revalidate: the next read still gets the stale value while fresh data loads in the background, and the action response does not include a re-render. For read-your-own-writes after a mutation, call `updateTag` (or `revalidatePath`), which expires the data immediately so the same round trip renders the updated list.
reference: Next.js docs: Server Actions (revalidation); revalidateTag; updateTag

stem: Which two statements about `useFormStatus` are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: `data` holds the FormData being submitted, so a child can show what is being saved
options.why: The hook returns `pending`, `data`, `method` and `action` for the parent form.

options.text: It also reports pending status when the form's action is a client-side async function
options.why: It tracks any function passed to the form's action prop, not only Server Functions.

options.text: It reports the status of every form on the page, so one component can track all of them
options.why: It only tracks the nearest parent form of the component that calls it.

options.text: It returns an `isPending` boolean and the latest state returned by the action
options.why: That describes `useActionState`; useFormStatus does not expose the action's return value.

options.text: It must be imported from `react` and only works inside Server Components
options.why: It is imported from `react-dom` and is used in Client Components.

explanation: `useFormStatus()` (from `react-dom`) gives a component information about the last submission of its parent `<form>`: `pending`, `data` (FormData), `method` and `action`. It works with any function action. To get the action's return value, use `useActionState`.

stem:
A developer marks a component `'use client'` and writes `export default async function Profile() { const user = await getUser(); return

{user.name}

}`. What is the correct assessment?

options.text: This is fine: Client Components may be async as long as a Suspense boundary sits above them
options.why: Async components are a Server Component feature; Client Components must render synchronously.

options.text: Async Client Components are unsupported; use `use(promise)` or a Server Component
options.why: React warns that async/await is only supported in Server Components.

options.text: It works on the initial server render but fails after hydration, so it suits static pages only
options.why: It is unsupported in the browser; React does not await components during client rendering.

options.text: Next.js automatically converts async Client Components into Server Components at build time
options.why: The directive wins; Next.js does not silently move components across the boundary.

explanation: Only Server Components may be async functions. Client Components must render synchronously; React warns "async/await is not yet supported in Client Components". To read async data in a Client Component, pass in a promise and call `use(promise)` under a Suspense boundary, or use a data library. If the component needs no interactivity, drop `'use client'` and keep it a Server Component.
